transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood): Alright hi everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Samir, AE on the hosted team, and with me is Lena from our SE squad. We'll run through streaming behavior, common param patterns, and how you might handle retries and backpressure in a live app.

[00:18] Priya (Calyx): Hi thanks, we have limited time so mostly we want to understand how to keep clinician latency <200ms for short prompts and what happens when the stream drops. Also security questions.

[00:30] Lena (Redwood): Great, quick agenda: 1) live demo with the Conversation API, 2) parameter effects, 3) failure modes and retry cookbook, 4) Q&A. I'll start the demo and show a small browser client.

[00:45] Lena (Redwood): (typing) Okay I'm calling /v1/conversation with stream=true... you can see tokens arriving as server-sent events — each chunk is a delta, we keep the partial semantics simple so you can render incremental UI.

[01:12] Ethan (Calyx): When you say chunk, is that per-token or per-chunk of tokens? Like will we get 1 token messages flooding the client?

[01:22] Lena (Redwood): It's chunked based on runtime heuristics — small groups of tokens are grouped to avoid chattiness. We also expose a chunk_size hint in SDKs if you need tighter control. Note that network latency means first-byte time depends on model and sequence length.

[01:40] Samir (Redwood): One common wrinkle: if a client disconnects mid-stream we persist the partial KV cache server-side for a short window and allow a resume token to rehydrate — that's the resume flow. It's disabled by default but can be enabled for low-latency UIs.

[02:05] Marta (Calyx): Resume tokens — is that storing sensitive content? We need to keep PHI out of persistent caches.

[02:12] Lena (Redwood): Good callout. Resume token payloads are opaque handles; you can opt to encrypt them with your KMS or disable persistence entirely in Hosted. For HIPAA-adjacent customers we recommend Private or Dedicated with our VPC option, but many teams run with hosted + KMS and short TTLs.

[02:45] Priya (Calyx): Walk us through retries — like a mobile client losing connectivity in the middle of a clinician note. How should we reconnect without double actions?

[02:58] Lena (Redwood): Two patterns: idempotent retries and resume. For idempotency, include a client-generated idempotency_key with each request. If the client retries, the server detects duplicate operations and returns the same response or a 409-ish reconciliation response. For streaming resume, we issue a resume_id after the first successful handshake, and client can reconnect and request bytes after offset N.

[03:27] Samir (Redwood): And on the SDK side we provide a small helper: retryWithResume() that does exponential backoff with jitter, checks the resume_id, and reconciles partial UI state.

[03:40] Ethan (Calyx): Does resume increase token billing? If we re-stream tokens are they billed twice?

[03:48] Samir (Redwood): Good question — replays are not billed twice if they are a server-side resume (we mark them as replayed). If you issue a fresh generation the tokens will count again. We'll include details in the billing FAQ we share.

[04:05] Lena (Redwood): Now a quick demo of parameter effects. Temperature 0.0 for deterministic clinician templates, temperature 0.8 for creative suggestions. I'll run three requests in parallel: temp 0, temp 0.7, and top_p tweaks so you can see output variance.

[04:35] (demo outputs stream in browser)

[05:10] Marta (Calyx): For our use case we need deterministic summarization for patient notes. So we stick to temperature 0 or low top_p?

[05:18] Lena (Redwood): Exactly. Also pin max_tokens to sane limits, and use stop sequences where you control the shape of the output. For very strict templates we recommend combining with a small Reranker or a deterministic model variant.

[05:42] Priya (Calyx): On latency - how do hosted SLOs look? We need a 99th perc under 300ms for short prompts.

[05:50] Samir (Redwood): Hosted SLAs are tiered; typical short prompt latencies are model-dependent. We can provide performance profiles per model and region. For strict 99p SLA you might consider Redwood Dedicated with reserved pools; hosted can meet many production needs but dedicated is more predictable. We'll share our model latency matrix.

[06:20] Ethan (Calyx): Backpressure — what happens when we have spikes? Our web app will open many sockets.

[06:27] Lena (Redwood): Server and client cooperatively handle backpressure. On the server we prioritize by route and token budget, and expose a 429/Retry-After header. On the client we have SDK helpers to pause reading and apply local rate-limiting. For very bursty traffic you can configure autoscaling and burst capacity on Dedicated. Hosted will throttle with clear signals.

[06:55] Priya (Calyx): You mentioned livetrace earlier — can you show logs/traces per request? We need audit trails for reviewer flows.

[07:05] Lena (Redwood): Sure — in the Console Livetrace view you can see per-request spans: handshake, model_infer, stream_emit, and finalization. We also surface token-level timing so you can pinpoint slow kernels. Demo: opening the Console now... (screen share) — here is a sample trace showing a slow model_infer span due to long context length.

[07:40] Samir (Redwood): That trace also links to config: model_version, quantization profile, batch_size, and the route policy. Very helpful for troubleshooting regressions.

[08:02] Marta (Calyx): Any advanced tuning you recommend? We plan to use 512 token contexts mostly.

[08:10] Lena (Redwood): For 512 tokens, enable KV caching and tune batch_size to reduce per-token cost but keep latency low. Try dynamic batching hints — and for safety enable prefix caching for identical system prompts. We'll provide a recommended config sheet.

[08:32] Ethan (Calyx): Security checklist — SSO, SAML, audit logs, retention policies — do you have a compliance pack?

[08:40] Samir (Redwood): Yes, we have a security pack. Hosted supports SAML SSO, role-based access controls, and audit logging. For KMS integration we support customer-managed keys through cloud KMS and HSM options in Private. We'll send the SOC 2 and encryption docs.

[09:00] Priya (Calyx): Great. Can we do a small benchmark — 1k short prompts/day — to see latency tail?

[09:08] Samir (Redwood): Absolutely. Typical POC plan: 1) define workload and test harness, 2) Redwood runs a 48-72 hr baseline in hosted region, 3) analyze traces and recommend tuning. We can get that scheduled.

[09:28] (Demo resumes to show a simulated disconnect and resume)

[10:05] Lena (Redwood): Example code: client opens stream, receives resume_id in meta, if socket drops we call reconnect with resume_id and offset. The reconnect flow is idempotent and the SDK handles merging deltas.

[10:30] Speaker 3: (muffled) Are there costs for enabling resume?

[10:36] Samir (Redwood): Minimal — resume state TTL is configurable; storage of resume handles is inexpensive. We'll include specifics in the cost appendix.

[10:50] Priya (Calyx): On the topic of partial responses—if we render partial to UI and the model later edits the earlier text, do you support edit deltas?

[11:00] Lena (Redwood): We stream deltas including edit ops; the client can apply patches. We also expose message-level checksums so you can validate sequence integrity.

[11:20] Marta (Calyx): Competitors — we've been evaluating other vendors and self-hosted stacks. Any differentiation to call out?

[11:28] Samir (Redwood): Short list: 1) unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, 2) livetrace + token-level timing tied to config, and 3) built-in resume/idempotency tooling. We'll send a competitor FAQ; many commercial vendors don't expose the same trace fidelity or resume helpers.

[11:50] Ethan (Calyx): Any gotchas for mobile clients?

[11:56] Lena (Redwood): Mobile should use short-lived resumable sessions, be conservative with long context, and implement local queueing to avoid bursts. We have an SDK snippet for React Native.

[12:12] Priya (Calyx): Can you show an example retry policy?

[12:18] Lena (Redwood): Sure: initial delay 200ms, max delay 5s, exponential backoff factor 2, jitter 0.25, stop after 5 attempts. For streaming we prefer resume within 10s to avoid large replays.

[12:38] (client code snippet read aloud)

[13:00] Marta (Calyx): If we move to Dedicated later, will our client code change?

[13:06] Samir (Redwood): Minimal changes — same Conversation API surface. Mostly config changes: endpoint, auth, and route policies. We'll support seamless switch with pinned model versions.

[13:25] Priya (Calyx): Ok let's go through the checklist and next steps.

[13:30] Samir (Redwood): Recap: We showed streaming tokens, resume, idempotency, backpressure signals, livetrace, and recommended param settings for deterministic summarization. Next we'll share security docs, the perf matrix, and a short POC plan.

[13:50] Ethan (Calyx): Sounds good. Interested in a week-long pilot focusing on short prompts and 99p latency.

[14:00] Samir (Redwood): Great — we'll propose dates and a test harness. Any final questions?

[14:08] Priya (Calyx): One last: data residency — can hosted pin region to EU?

[14:14] Lena (Redwood): Yes, you can choose region and we support region-restricted storage. For stronger requirements we recommend Private with on-prem or VPC.

[14:30] Marta (Calyx): Thank you, that was helpful.

[14:34] Samir (Redwood): Thanks everyone — we'll follow up.

[14:38] (meeting ends)
